name: Aramaic
region: Syria and Mesopotamia, then the whole Near East from Egypt to Afghanistan; today scattered communities in Syria, Iraq, Turkey and Iran and in diaspora
defining_innovation: Proto-Semitic *ð merged with d: Aramaic dəhav 'gold' beside Hebrew zāhāv and Arabic ḏahab.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
Aramaic first appears in inscriptions of the small Aramean kingdoms of Syria in the 10th–9th centuries BCE. It then became something much larger. The Assyrian empire deported and resettled Aramaic speakers across its territory, and Aramaic spread as the everyday language of the empire. The Babylonians and then the Achaemenid Persians used it as their administrative language from Egypt to India. Parts of the biblical books of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic, and it was the everyday language of Judea in the time of Jesus.

Aramaic merged some Proto-Semitic consonants differently from Hebrew: `*ð` became *d*, so 'gold' is *dəhav* against Hebrew *zāhāv*.

chapters.title: A Script for Half of Asia
chapters.body: The Aramaic alphabet had even wider descendants than the language. Jews adopted it for Hebrew, and the 'square' Hebrew letters are Aramaic in origin. The Nabataeans developed a cursive form of it that became the Arabic script. Syriac, Mandaic and Palmyrene scripts are Aramaic, and so are the Kharosthi script of northwest India and the Sogdian script of Central Asia. Sogdian in turn gave rise to the Old Uyghur script on the Turkic tree, and through it to Mongolian and Manchu writing.

chapters.title: Syriac and Neo-Aramaic
chapters.body:
The Aramaic of Edessa, **Syriac**, became the literary language of Christianity in the east from the 2nd century CE. Its missionaries took it to India and China: a bilingual Chinese–Syriac stele was set up in Xi'an in 781. After the Arab conquests, Arabic gradually replaced Aramaic as the spoken language of the region. The **Neo-Aramaic** languages of today survived in mountain villages and among Christian, Jewish and Mandaean minorities.

The 20th and 21st centuries have been devastating: massacres during the First World War, and war and emigration from Iraq and Syria, have scattered the remaining speakers. Western Neo-Aramaic survives in Maaloula and two neighbouring villages near Damascus.

turning_points.title: *ð merges with d
turning_points.description: Proto-Semitic `*ð` merges with `d`: Aramaic *dəhav* 'gold' against Hebrew *zāhāv* and Arabic *ḏahab*. The earliest inscriptions write it with the letter for *z*, which suggests the merger came after the script was borrowed.

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Language of empires
turning_points.description: Assyria, then Babylon, then Achaemenid Persia use Aramaic as the everyday and administrative language of their empires. It replaces Akkadian and is written from Egypt to Afghanistan.

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Spirantisation of b g d k p t
turning_points.description: After vowels, the stops `b g d k p t` become fricatives `v ɣ ð x f θ`. The change spreads to Hebrew, and the Tiberian vowel signs record it in the Hebrew Bible. Its date and whether it began in Aramaic are debated.
turning_points.notation: b g d k p t → v ɣ ð x f θ / V_

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.
Sáenz-Badillos, Angel. 1993. A History of the Hebrew Language. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: The Aramaic script family
turning_points.description: The Aramaic alphabet becomes the parent of the Hebrew square script, Nabataean (and so Arabic), Syriac, Mandaic and Sogdian. Through Sogdian it leads to the Old Uyghur, Mongolian and Manchu scripts.

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Syriac Christianity travels east
turning_points.description: Syriac becomes the literary language of the churches of the east, and its missionaries reach India, Central Asia and China. The Xi'an stele of 781 is inscribed in Chinese and Syriac.

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Arabic replaces Aramaic
turning_points.description: After the Arab conquests, Arabic becomes the everyday language of Syria and Mesopotamia over several centuries. Aramaic survives mainly in villages and in liturgy.

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Massacre, war and diaspora
turning_points.description: Massacres during the First World War and later wars in Iraq and Syria scatter the Neo-Aramaic-speaking communities, and many now live in diaspora in Europe, North America and Australia. Several Neo-Aramaic varieties have only elderly speakers.

sources.citation: Weninger, Stefan, ed. 2011. The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
